transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2027-02-14 08:00 PT
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Platform: Zoom

Summary (auto):
Quick discovery focused on p95 latency and surge throughput for Reverie Logistics’ chat-assist and routing features. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, streaming token/sec benchmarks, KV cache reuse, and security/audit needs. Agreed next steps: share perf runbook, customer to provide traffic trace, schedule benchmark window.

Topics (auto):
- p95 targets & SLOs
- Concurrency (active sessions) & cold start behavior
- Streaming vs chunked tokenization
- Dedicated pool sizing and fallback strategies
- Security: VPC, KMS, SOC2/audit logs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya, AE on the account, with Ethan from our SE team.
[00:07] Lena Ortiz: Hi, thanks. I'm Lena, CTO at Reverie. Wanted to make sure we dive straight into the numbers — p95 goals, what shipping looks like under real traffic.
[00:15] Maya Chen: Perfect. Can you frame the app surface? Heard it's a driver-chat assistant and a routing hint generator?
[00:21] Lena Ortiz: Yeah, two main pieces. The chat assistant is customer-visible, streaming responses to mobile apps, typical utterance lengths of 120–300 tokens. Routing hints is short responses but high concurrency spikes — like 6k rps for a minute during rush.
[00:36] Harold Ng: Right — the routing requests are usually 16–32 tokens but extremely bursty. Our p95 SLA for critical routing calls needs to be <= 120ms. For chat p95 we'd like <= 600ms.
[00:48] Ethan Park: Okay that's useful. Quick clarification: are those numbers measured end-to-end from client or from your API gateway?
[00:53] Priya Shah: From our gateway — so includes network hop within our VPC to wherever the model runs. We need to factor network egress and TLS.
[01:02] Ethan Park: Got it. So when we talk about p95 at 120ms, that is tight. For tiny payloads and short contexts we can hit sub-100ms on Dedicated with NVLink-backed GPUs depending on model choice and quantization. For Hosted, typical network and multi-tenant noise can make the tail wider, so we usually guide customers to Dedicated for strict sub-200ms p95.
[01:20] Lena Ortiz: Is that because of noisy neighbors? Or routing and queuing in the hosted fabric?
[01:25] Maya Chen: Both. Hosted is optimized for developer velocity and lower unit cost. It's multi-tenant so there is some scheduling and preemption. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity, deterministic batching windows, and can take advantage of pinned kernels and lower queueing.
[01:37] [01:40] Marco Silva: We also care about streaming behaviour. Our mobile client expects tokens sent asap; ideally the first token within 150ms. How do you measure cold start vs warm prefixes?
[01:49] Ethan Park: For streaming, prefix KV-cache is critical. In Dedicated we can keep the KV cache warm across sessions if you opt for long-lived workers. Cold start comes from weight load and memory eviction. We usually recommend an LRU warm-warm policy and a small warm pool for high-priority routes.
[02:05] Maya Chen: One practical thing — when you provide us the 24h trace, include percentage of streaming sessions and average session duration so we can propose a warm pool size.
[02:13] Priya Shah: Sure. Another question — we are exploring VPC private deployment for compliance. Latency wise, does Private (VPC) look closer to Dedicated or Hosted?
[02:23] Ethan Park: Private sits in between. If you're deploying in your VPC with our Private control plane and GPUs in your cloud account, network latency depends on your infra. But the runtime characteristics are similar to Dedicated since it's single-tenant from the inference perspective. The big difference is operational overhead for you.
[02:37] Harold Ng: For the 6k rps spike, what's the recommended fallback? Can Redwood do autoscale burst capacity or spill to a cheaper model variant?
[02:46] Ethan Park: Yes — we have a routing policy: active pool, burst pool, and a fallback to quantized or smaller model variants. For example, you can route critical routing calls to a low-latency optimized tiny model on Dedicated; less critical calls hit the regular model. Autoscale burst is available but has cold-start constraints — it's better to provision a burst buffer.
[03:03] Lena Ortiz: Can you give an example tokens/sec numbers? We did some internal tests on gpt-like open models and saw ~800 tokens/sec on a single A10G for streaming contexts, but that was with batching.
[03:16] Ethan Park: Sure, ballpark: on an A100-class VM with optimized kernels and 8-bit quantization, for a medium-sized model (7B-ish) you might see 2k–4k tokens/sec with moderate batching. For smaller low-latency models you can get higher tokens/sec per GPU. But the user-perceived latency for streaming is dominated by first-token latency and prefix lookup.
[03:35] [03:36] Priya Shah: So to hit our 120ms p95 for routing we likely need a custom small model?
[03:41] Maya Chen: Likely. We can help with model selection. Often customers use a hybrid approach: tiny model for decisioning, larger for explanation/chat.
[03:49] Marco Silva: About batching — our routing calls are single-request single-token workloads. Batching hurts latency there. How does Redwood handle continuous batching without penalizing ultra-low-latency calls?
[03:59] Ethan Park: Continuous batching is workload-aware. You can define priority lanes and a latency SLO. For the high-priority lane we set a very short batching window (1–2ms) to basically avoid queueing; for lower priority lanes we allow longer windows to improve throughput. That behavior is configurable per-route.
[04:15] Lena Ortiz: Can we see the per-route latency breakdown (model compute, queueing, network)?
[04:19] Maya Chen: Yes, Console gives token-level breakdowns and tracing hooks. We'll include screenshots in the runbook.
[04:26] Harold Ng: Security — SOC2, KMS, and audit logs important. We need to know who touched the keys and ability to rotate.
[04:33] Noah Ruiz: We can integrate with your KMS (GCP KMS, AWS KMS, HSM) and provide audit logs for inference requests. For Private deployments we support customer-managed keys and HSM attachments. Hosted has managed keys but we provide key access logs.
[04:47] Priya Shah: What about data retention and ability to disable training on logs?
[04:51] Maya Chen: By default we do not use customer data to train models. You can configure retention policies and turn off telemetry forwarding. We'll include that in the SOC2 pack.
[04:59] Marco Silva: Back to the numbers — when you provision Dedicated pool, is the token/sec linear with number of GPUs? Or are there diminishing returns due to model parallelism?
[05:09] Ethan Park: Good question. For small models (single-GPU), scaling is near linear if you split by requests across workers. Large models with model-parallel setups need careful kernel-level tuning. For your workload (mostly small models for routing + medium chat models), you would likely run multiple single-GPU workers and see near-linear throughput per GPU.
[05:26] [05:27] Lena Ortiz: Cold start worst-case numbers? If a new worker spins up to handle burst, what's the cold start delta on p95?
[05:33] Ethan Park: Cold start from scratch (load weights) can add 200–800ms depending on model size and image pull. If you pre-warm images and keep a tiny warm pool you can reduce cold start to ~30–80ms due to memory/weight residency. That's why we suggest a warm buffer for routing-critical lanes.
[05:50] Maya Chen: We'll sketch a warm buffer recommendation once we see the trace.
[05:55] Priya Shah: One more: quantization quality tradeoffs — how aggressive can we go for routing? Are hallucinations a concern?
[06:02] Ethan Park: For routing, since outputs are constrained and short, 4-bit or mixed 8-bit quantization often works fine. We recommend an eval set to validate. For chat where quality matters, you'd use less aggressive quantization or reranking. Redwood Optimize can give suggestions based on your evals.
[06:20] Lena Ortiz: Does Redwood support reranking as a managed stage? Like run cheap model then re-score with larger model?
[06:25] Ethan Park: Yes — function chaining and reranking pipelines are supported. You can use an initial low-latency model to propose candidates and a heavier model for scoring in the background.
[06:34] [06:35] Marco Silva: On the benchmarking side, what does Redwood need? We can provide synthetic load or live-traff trace.
[06:41] Maya Chen: Both are useful. For sizing, a 24h trace is best because it captures diurnal patterns and microbursts. For pure tokens/sec numbers, synthetic runs with representative prompt distribution are fine. Please include percent streaming sessions, payload sizes, and any burst window definitions.
[06:55] Harold Ng: Cost question — if we provision a big warm buffer for routing, what's the bill implications? Is there a cheaper preemptible option for burst?
[07:02] Ethan Park: Warm buffer is reserved capacity so it's charged as reserved Dedicated capacity. You can lean on burst capacity that uses lower-priority GPUs (cheaper) but cold start is longer. We can model cost impact in the pricing matrix we'll send.
[07:14] Lena Ortiz: For the 6k rps spike — what's a realistic Dedicated footprint? Any back-of-envelope?
[07:21] Ethan Park: Rough back-of-envelope: if routing calls are ~20 tokens and each request is single-shot with near-zero batching, you need many workers. If a single GPU worker can handle ~8000 requests/sec for tiny models (this varies a lot), then you might need under one GPU; but that's optimistic. More conservatively, estimate 2000–4000 rps per GPU for tiny models depending on network. We'll compute a tighter estimate once we see the trace and your average token lengths.
[07:45] Priya Shah: Could you put those assumptions in writing? We need numbers for our SRE capacity plan.
[07:49] Maya Chen: Absolutely — that's in the perf runbook and the Dedicated sizing sketch Ethan will do.
[07:54] [08:00] Marco Silva: Any limitations on websocket streaming? We use mobile clients with flaky networks. We need graceful reconnection and partial token replay.
[08:09] Ethan Park: Websocket streaming is fully supported. We have resumable streaming tokens based on per-session KV checkpointing. On reconnection we can replay the last few tokens or resume from a checkpoint. We'll include sample code.
[08:21] Lena Ortiz: For our security team, can we get a short IRL audit path? Like who accessed what model weights and logs?
[08:28] Noah Ruiz: Yes — audit logs include call metadata, user identities, and KMS key access events. For Private, since you run in your account, you can combine our logs with your cloud audit logs.
[08:39] [08:40] Harold Ng: OK let's talk timeline. We want a pilot in Q2. How long to proof?
[08:45] Maya Chen: Typical pilot is 4–6 weeks: initial sizing and bench in week 1–2, integration and security checks in week 2–4, and runway for smoothing in weeks 4–6. If you provide the traffic trace quickly we can accelerate the sizing.
[08:58] Priya Shah: Sounds good.
[09:00] Maya Chen: Any other blockers?
[09:02] Lena Ortiz: One unresolved is legal procurement timing. Procurement might need a SOC2 package and DPA before any data is routed.
[09:09] Maya Chen: We'll surface the SOC2/ISO pack and redwood DPA template. Noah will own delivering that.
[09:15] [09:18] Marco Silva: Last minor thing — can you do a short stress test where you route 10k rps for 30s and capture p95 tail? We want an empirical number not just estimates.
[09:27] Ethan Park: Yes — we can run a controlled stress test in a reserved Dedicated window. We prefer synthetic replay of your trace to get realistic queuing patterns.
[09:34] Lena Ortiz: Great. Thanks everyone.
[09:36] Maya Chen: Recap (auto): Maya to share perf runbook and pricing matrix; Priya to supply 24h trace; Ethan to produce Dedicated sizing sketch and propose benchmark window; Noah to attach security docs. We'll circle back with a calendar invite for the 2-hour bench.
[09:51] Harold Ng: Thanks, appreciate it.
[09:53] Maya Chen: Thanks all.

End of transcript.
